sites.s: Bronze Age tower and Iron Age town near Bisya · Italian Mission to Oman
sites.p: Early Bronze Age to Iron Age (reused to the Islamic period)
sites.te: The hill where legends and layers meet
sites.ta: التلّ الذي تلتقي فيه الأساطير بالطبقات
sites.se: A fortified hill and a lower town near Bisya, dug since 2004 by an Italian mission, with a Bronze Age tower and an Iron Age settlement far larger than once thought
sites.sa: تلّ محصّن ومدينة سفلية قرب بسيا، تنقّب فيهما بعثة إيطالية منذ 2004، مع برج من العصر البرونزي ومستوطنة من العصر الحديدي أكبر بكثير مما كان يُظن
sites.desc: An ancient oasis on the Salut plain near Bisya in central Oman, first surveyed in the 1970s by Harvard University, the British Archaeological Expedition and the University of Birmingham, and excavated from 2004 by the Italian Mission to Oman (IMTO) led by Alessandra Avanzini. The mission rebuilt a collapsed Bronze Age tower, plastered the mud-brick walls for preservation and, after a decade of work, had restored the site's monumentality by 2015. Excavation of the lower settlement (Qaryat Salut) showed its inhabited area was much larger than previously thought, and very high radiocarbon dates from the upper fortified area (Husn Salut) point to a large central-Omani settlement by the end of the 2nd millennium BC with classic Iron Age material culture. Finds include pottery, soft-stone vessels, seals, bronze objects and terracotta figurines, presented in a Virtual Museum of Salut built by the mission.
sites.sig: Salut is the key excavated sequence for the Iron Age of central Oman, a region long overshadowed by sites in the UAE.
sites.ex: Italian Mission to Oman (University of Pisa, A. Avanzini) 2004–present; earlier surveys by Harvard, the British Archaeological Expedition and University of Birmingham
disc: Iron Age lower town far larger than previously thought
Bronze Age tower rebuilt after collapse
refs: Tagliamonte, E. & Avanzini, A. (2018). New data from the renewed excavation at Salūt: the Iron Age settlement (Qaryat Salūt). Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 48, 339–353.
Oman Observer (2024). Salut: A glimpse into Oman's ancient heritage.

sites.s: Hafit-period towers with the oldest copper working in Oman · University of Tübingen
sites.el: Building V dated to about 3200 cal. BC
sites.ta: حيث صُهر النحاس في عُمان أول مرة
sites.se: One of the largest Early Bronze Age sites in Oman, 17 km north of Sinaw, whose stone tower holds the oldest substantial evidence of copper processing in the country
sites.sa: أحد أكبر مواقع العصر البرونزي المبكر في عُمان، على بعد 17 كم شمال سناو، يضم برجه الحجري أقدم دليل جوهري على معالجة النحاس في البلاد
sites.desc: Al-Khashbah, about 17 km north of Sinaw, is one of Oman's largest Early Bronze Age sites. The University of Tübingen excavated there for four seasons from 2015 to 2018 and uncovered Hafit-period architecture including a mud-brick complex (Building I, dated to about 2800 cal. BC) with bead and chipped-stone workshops, resembling the contemporary tower at Hili 8, and a stone tower (Building V) dated to about 3200 cal. BC. Building V holds the oldest substantial evidence of copper processing in Oman, which the excavators link to archaic Uruk texts that mention copper objects from the Arabian Gulf. The site has three Hafit-period stone towers and six Umm an-Nar-period towers, and the project, funded by the German Research Foundation, combined field, aerial and geophysical surveys with excavation.
sites.sig: It pushes the beginning of Omani copper metallurgy, the basis of the land of Magan, back to the end of the 4th millennium BC.
sites.ex: University of Tübingen (C. Schmidt, S. Döpper), 2015–2018
disc: Oldest substantial copper processing in Oman, c. 3200 BC
Mud-brick complex with bead workshops, c. 2800 BC
refs: Schmidt, C. & Döpper, S. (2019). The Hafit period at Al-Khashbah, Sultanate of Oman: results of four years of excavations and material studies. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 49, 265–274.

Schmidt, C. & Döpper, S. (2017). The development of complexity at third-millennium BC al-Khashbah, Sultanate of Oman: results of the first two seasons, 2015 and 2016. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 47, 215–227.

sites.s: Neolithic fishing village and shell midden in Muscat · Italian Archaeological Mission
sites.se: A shell-midden village on a promontory at Qurm, Muscat, where Neolithic fisher-gatherers lived year-round and buried their dead in a large cemetery
sites.sa: قرية من أكوام الأصداف على رأس بحري في القرم بمسقط، عاش فيها صيادون وجامعو أصداف من العصر الحجري الحديث طوال العام ودفنوا موتاهم في مقبرة كبيرة
sites.desc: RH-5 is a shell-midden settlement on a large promontory in the Qurm area of Muscat, excavated by the Italian Archaeological Mission in Oman with the support of the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism. It dates from the late 5th to the end of the 4th millennium BC and consists of superimposed food refuse from fishing, shell collecting, hunting and herding, together with dwellings, household installations, everyday objects and ornaments. Exploiting several ecological niches allowed year-round sedentary occupation. The excavations recovered 374 beads of stone and marine shell, and the site includes a large cemetery.
sites.sig: It is the reference site for the fisher-gatherer way of life that the excavators see as a key step in the neolithisation of Oman.
sites.ex: Italian Archaeological Mission in Oman (P. Biagi; later L. G. Marcucci, É. Badel, F. Genchi), Ministry of Heritage and Tourism
refs: Marcucci, L. G., Badel, É. & Genchi, F. (2021). Prehistoric fisherfolk of Oman: the Neolithic village of Ras Al-Hamra RH-5. Archaeopress, Oxford.
Pisan, A., Biagi, P. & Gasparotto, G. Stone and shell beads from the shell-midden settlement RH-5, Muscat (Sultanate of Oman). Harappa.com.

sites.s: Largest Early Iron Age hill fort in central Oman · German Mining Museum survey
sites.el: Fort surface of more than 20,000 m²
sites.te: A staircase up a mountain of stone
sites.se: A ruined stone fort about 175 m wide on a mountain top near the Lizq palm garden, reached by a stair up its northern face
sites.sa: حصن حجري متهدّم بعرض نحو 175 م على قمة جبل قرب بستان نخيل لزق، يُصعد إليه بدرج على واجهته الشمالية
sites.desc: The fort known as L1 stands on a mountain about 1,000 m south-east of the Lizq palm garden in Ash Sharqiyah North. The main fort on the western peak is about 175 m wide with a surface of more than 20,000 m², and stairs lead up the northern face of the mountain. Gerd Weisgerber of the German Mining Museum in Bochum discovered it in 1979, guided by Shaikh Hamdan al-Harthy of Samad, and in 1981 a single-season German team under Stephan Kroll mapped the site, carried out a small rescue excavation and restored the northern stairs. Kroll compared its pottery with Iron Age pottery from Iran; no falaj was found and the associated village has not been located.
sites.sig: It is described as the largest Early Iron Age fort in central Oman.
sites.ex: German Mining Museum, Bochum (G. Weisgerber 1979; S. Kroll 1981)
disc: Stone stairway up the northern face
refs: Kroll, S. (2013). The Early Iron Age Lizq Fort, Sultanate of Oman. Zeitschrift für Archäologie Außereuropäischer Kulturen 5.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Lizq, citing Kroll (1998, 2013) and Yule (2001).

sites.s: Type-site of the Samad Late Iron Age · about 260 graves documented
sites.el: About 260 graves, Bronze Age to Late Iron Age
sites.se: An oasis cemetery in Sharqiyah where German excavations defined the non-writing Late Iron Age culture of central Oman
sites.sa: مقبرة واحة في الشرقية حدّدت فيها التنقيبات الألمانية ثقافة العصر الحديدي المتأخر غير الكاتبة في وسط عُمان
sites.desc: Samad al-Shan is an oasis about 2 km east of al-Maysar in Sharqiyah at 565 m altitude, discovered in part by British surveyors in 1976. From 1981 Gerd Weisgerber of the German Mining Museum in Bochum mapped it, and Burkhard Vogt, Weisgerber and Paul Yule excavated there; by the end of the project in 1995 about 210 of some 360 Late Iron Age graves had been investigated, and roughly 260 graves from the Bronze Age to the Late Iron Age were documented. The Samad assemblage, now known from 126 sites, is dated by absolute methods to about 300 BC – AD 300. Mature men were usually laid on the right side and women on the left; men's graves hold arrowheads, daggers and swords, women's never contain weapons, and imported glazed perfume bottles and lathe-turned soft-stone bowls appear with hand-made local pottery.
sites.sig: The site gives its name to the Late Iron Age of central Oman, a period otherwise without writing.
sites.ex: German Mining Museum, Bochum, later University of Heidelberg (G. Weisgerber, B. Vogt, P. Yule), 1981–1995
disc: About 210 of 360 Late Iron Age graves excavated
Men buried on the right, women on the left
refs: Yule, P. (2001). Die Gräberfelder in Samad al-Shan (Sultanat Oman). Materialien zu einer Kulturgeschichte. Rahden.
Yule, P. (2008). Sasanian Presence and Late Iron Age Samad in Central Oman, some Corrections. Heidelberg University.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Samad al-Shan, citing Yule (2001, 2016, 2018).

sites.s: 17th-century round tower of the Ya’ariba imams · Nizwa
sites.el: Tower about 36 m across and 30 m high
sites.te: A drum of stone over an underground stream
sites.ta: أسطوانة من حجر فوق جدول تحت الأرض
sites.se: A huge round tower built in the 1650s under Imam Sultan bin Saif, filled with rubble and ringed by 480 gun-ports
sites.sa: برج دائري ضخم بُني في خمسينيات القرن السابع عشر في عهد الإمام سلطان بن سيف، مملوء بالردم ومحاط بـ480 فتحة للبنادق
sites.desc: Nizwa Fort was built in the 1650s under Imam Sultan bin Saif, the second Ya'rubi ruler, over an underlying structure of the 12th century; the main work took about 12 years. The round tower is about 36 m in diameter and 30 m high (official tourism figures give 45 m and 34 m), its foundations go about 30 m into the ground, and part of it is filled with rocks, dirt and rubble above an underground stream. Defences include murder holes above the doors, about 24 openings for mortar fire, 480 gun-ports, 24 original cannons of which four remain, pitfalls in the twisting stair and cellars for food and munitions. One cannon from Boston was presented to the first Omani ambassador to the United States in 1840.
sites.sig: It is the best-known of Oman's forts and the seat from which the Ya'ariba imams ruled the interior.
sites.ex: Built under Imam Sultan bin Saif al-Ya’rubi; managed as a heritage site by Oman (Omran)
refs: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Nizwa Fort, citing Experience Oman, Walker (Lonely Planet 2007) and Cox, P. (1925) The Geographical Journal 66(3).
Experience Oman (Ministry of Heritage and Tourism). Nizwa Fort.

sites.s: Painted-ceiling palace of Imam Bilarab bin Sultan · Bahla
sites.se: A five-storey palace of plastered sandstone built in 1670 by Imam Bilarab bin Sultan, famed for ceilings painted with calligraphy and a Sun and Moon room with 14 windows
sites.sa: قصر من خمسة طوابق من الحجر الرملي المُجصّص بناه الإمام بلعرب بن سلطان عام 1670، يشتهر بسقوفه المزخرفة بالخط العربي وبغرفة الشمس والقمر ذات الـ14 نافذة
sites.desc: Jabrin Castle stands among farms in the Wilayat of Bahla, Al Dakhiliyah. It was built in 1670 by Imam Bilarab bin Sultan bin Saif al-Ya'rubi, third of the Ya'ariba imams, from grey sandstone covered in thick plaster, with five floors and 55 rooms around two courtyards 16 and 22 m high, each with a well more than 20 m deep. Many rooms have ceilings painted with Arabic calligraphy; the Sun and Moon room has 14 windows, the upper ones admitting moonlight and the lower controlling daylight, and the imam's protection room contains four secret trenches. Two towers defended it, a falaj waters the orchards, and it served first as the imam's palace and later as a seat of government; it also held a library, a courtroom and a classroom for Quran lessons, and the imam was buried in a corner of the ground floor.
sites.sig: It is the finest example of Omani palace decoration from the Ya'ariba period.
sites.ex: Built under Imam Bilarab bin Sultan; open daily as a heritage site
disc: Sun and Moon room with 14 windows
refs: Oman Observer (2024). Jabreen Castle's painted ceilings attract visitors.
Oman Observer (2017). The Persistence of Jabreen Castle.

sites.s: 5 km karst cave with an underground lake and blind fish · show cave since 2006
sites.p: Karst in Cretaceous limestone of the Hajar
sites.se: A 5 km cave at the foot of Jebel Shams, believed to be 2 million years old, whose lake is home to the Omani blind cave fish
sites.sa: كهف بطول 5 كم عند سفح جبل شمس يُعتقد أن عمره مليونا سنة، تعيش في بحيرته سمكة الكهف العُمانية العمياء
sites.desc: Al Hoota Cave lies at Al Hamra in Ad Dakhiliyah at the foot of Jebel Shams. The karst system is about 5 km long, of which 4.5 km is show cave, with its highest point about 65 m above the entrance; it is believed to be about two million years old and opened to visitors in 2006 with electric lighting and a guided walk of 500 m ending at an underground lake 800 m long. The lake holds the Omani blind cave fish (Garra barreimiae), whose adults lose their eyesight, and the cave shelters more than 100 animal species including bats, hunter spiders and water beetles. Its stalagmites have been used for palaeoclimate research, including a 2022 Science study on droughts in late antique Arabia.
sites.sig: It is Oman's only developed show cave and a natural archive of past climate.
sites.ex: Managed as a show cave (opened 2006); stalagmites studied by D. Fleitmann et al.
refs: Fleitmann, D. et al. (2022). Droughts and societal change: The environmental context for the emergence of Islam in late antique Arabia. Science 376, 1317–1321.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Al Hoota Cave, citing BBC (2012) and Toronto Star (2009).

sites.s: Collapse sinkhole in coastal limestone · Hawiyat Najm Park
sites.el: About 50 by 70 m wide and 20 m deep
sites.te: The well of the falling star
sites.se: A sinkhole 50 by 70 m across and 20 m deep, 600 m from the sea, formed when the roof of dissolved limestone collapsed; locals once blamed a meteorite
sites.sa: بلعة بعرض 50 في 70 م وعمق 20 م على بعد 600 م من البحر، تكوّنت عندما انهار سقف الحجر الجيري المذاب؛ وكان الأهالي يعزونها إلى نيزك
sites.desc: Hawiyat Najm, 'the deep well of the falling star', lies between Dibab and Bimmah on the Muscat–Sur highway, about 600 m from the sea. The sinkhole is roughly 50 m by 70 m across and about 20 m deep, and formed when the surface layer collapsed as the underlying limestone dissolved. The name records a local belief that a meteorite made it. The municipality has developed Hawiyat Najm Park around it, fenced, with a stairway down to the water.
sites.sig: It is the most accessible example of karst collapse on Oman's eastern coast.
sites.ex: Hawiyat Najm Park (local municipality); limestone mapped by S. Rajendran & S. Nasir (2014)
disc: Named for a supposed fallen star
refs: Rajendran, S. & Nasir, S. (2014). ASTER mapping of limestone formations and study of caves, springs and depressions in parts of Sultanate of Oman. Environmental Earth Sciences 71(1), 133–146.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Bimmah Sinkhole, citing Oman Ministry of Tourism.

sites.s: Wind-sculpted limestone and sandstone about 40 million years old · Al Wusta
sites.se: Six square kilometres of limestone and sandstone laid down some 40 million years ago and eroded by wind and water into statue-like forms
sites.sa: ستة كيلومترات مربعة من الحجر الجيري والرملي ترسّبت قبل نحو 40 مليون سنة ونحتتها الرياح والمياه في أشكال تشبه التماثيل
sites.desc: The Rock Garden lies in the centre of Duqm, about 550 km from Muscat, inside the Special Economic Zone at Duqm. It covers about 6 km² of sandstone and limestone in which fragile limestone deposits, formed roughly 40 million years ago, are capped by a harder layer; wind and water erosion over millions of years sculpted them into symmetrical, statue-like forms. The site is fenced with visitor gates, parking and surveillance cameras and is run by the zone authority's Technical Affairs Department, which in 2024 commissioned a study for walkways and lighting. Admission is free.
sites.sig: It is described as one of the most important geological sites in Oman.
sites.ex: Special Economic Zone at Duqm (SEZAD), Technical Affairs Department
refs: Oman Observer (2024). Duqm Rock Garden: A geological marvel, tourist oasis.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Duqm Rock Garden, citing Times of Oman and Oman Observer (2017).

sites.s: Drowned valley of the sinking Musandam peninsula · 16 km long
sites.p: Jurassic Musandam Group limestone, drowned by Neogene subsidence
sites.dr: Collision began about 5 million years ago
sites.el: Peninsula sinking about 6 mm a year
sites.se: A 16 km inlet walled by 800 m cliffs, a river valley drowned as the Arabian plate bends down under Eurasia at 6 mm a year
sites.sa: خور بطول 16 كم تحيط به جروف بارتفاع 800 م، وادٍ نهري غمره البحر مع انثناء الصفيحة العربية تحت الصفيحة الأوراسية بمعدل 6 مم في السنة
sites.desc: Khor Ash Sham is the longest of the Musandam inlets, about 16 km long with walls rising about 800 m from the water. The inlets are rias, drowned river valleys that resemble fjords but were never carved by ice, since no glaciers have covered the Arabian Peninsula since the Permian; the peninsula is subsiding at about 6 mm a year as the Arabian lithosphere is flexed down beneath the Eurasian plate, in a collision that began about 5 million years ago. The cliffs are Jurassic Musandam Group carbonates about 1,500 m thick, with the Upper Triassic Ghalilah Formation exposed at sea level, and the Hagab Thrust records about 15 km of shortening. Telegraph Island in the inlet carries the foundations of a British cable repeater station built in 1865 and abandoned in 1868, and the khor has a healthy dolphin population.
sites.sig: It is the clearest place in Arabia to see a continent being pulled down into a plate collision.
sites.ex: Geology described by L. Abbott & T. Cook (GeoExpro 2020)
disc: Subsidence of about 6 mm a year
Cliffs of Jurassic limestone 800 m high
refs: Abbott, L. & Cook, T. (2020). Oman's Musandam Peninsula: Geodynamic and Geopolitical Nexus. GeoExpro.
Rough Guides. The khors and Kumzar: Khor Ash Sham.

sites.s: Oman Exotic limestone block with a 1,000 m south face · Wadi al-Ayn
sites.p: Permian–Triassic Oman Exotic limestone, thrust onto Arabia in the Late Cretaceous
sites.te: A reef that sank, then rose
sites.se: A 2,090 m comb-shaped mountain of exotic limestone, a sunken reef platform carried onto Arabia when the Tethys closed, with a near-vertical face over 1,000 m
sites.sa: جبل على شكل مشط بارتفاع 2,090 م من الحجر الجيري الدخيل، منصة شعابية غارقة حُملت على شبه الجزيرة العربية عند انغلاق محيط تيثس، بواجهة شبه عمودية تتجاوز 1,000 م
sites.desc: Jebel Misht, 'Comb Mountain', rises to 2,090 m above Wadi al-Ayn about 50 km north-west of Nizwa, with a south face of over 1,000 m rising almost vertically. It is made of Oman Exotic Limestone, a block out of sequence with the surrounding rocks that was thrust onto Arabia when the Tethys Ocean closed about 65 million years ago. The Oman Exotics are limestones caught up in the thrust stack beneath the Semail Ophiolite; the Middle–Late Permian ones were reef build-ups on platforms that sank to ocean depths during rifting and were later engulfed by basalts, and carry foraminifera, calcareous algae, corals and crinoids. Michael Searle, Peter King and Philip Davis made the first recorded ascent by the west ridge on 11–12 February 1982, and the south face was climbed in February 1983.
sites.sig: It is the most dramatic of Oman's exotic blocks, a piece of Tethyan sea floor standing on the desert edge.
sites.ex: Geology by M. P. Searle; Permian exotics studied by O. Abdelghany, A. R. Fowler & W. Hashem (2019)
disc: Exotic limestone out of sequence with its surroundings
refs: Searle, M. P. (1985). Arabian Fantasy – Jebel Misht. American Alpine Journal.

Abdelghany, O., Fowler, A. R. & Hashem, W. (2019). Oman Exotic limestones in the UAE-Oman border area with implications for Middle-Upper Permian Neo-Tethyan rifting. Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 181, 103879.

sites.s: Largest shorebird wetland in the Middle East · Ramsar site 2529
sites.te: Half a million birds on the mud
sites.se: A 2,137 km² peninsula of mudflats, seagrass and reef on the Arabian Sea where up to half a million waterbirds from Arctic Russia and Central Asia winter
sites.sa: شبه جزيرة بمساحة 2,137 كم² من المسطحات الطينية والأعشاب البحرية والشعاب على بحر العرب، يشتو فيها حتى نصف مليون طائر مائي قادم من روسيا القطبية وآسيا الوسطى
sites.desc: Barr Al Hikman in Mahout, Al Wusta, about 400 km south of Muscat, was made a nature reserve by Royal Decree 51/2014 and designated Ramsar site 2529 on 25 October 2023 with an area of 213,715 ha. A January 2016 count recorded 464,887 waterbirds, including 125,659 dunlin, 123,369 lesser sandplover and 60,976 bar-tailed godwit, and 18 species exceed 1% of their flyway populations; it is described as the most significant wintering wetland in the Middle East. Its Halodule and Halophila seagrass beds are the largest in Oman, with about 1,500 ha of coral reef and 200 ha of Avicennia mangrove, and the waters are used by the endangered Arabian Sea humpback whale and green and hawksbill turtles. Ten years of surveys by Wetlands International with Radboud University, Groningen, NIOZ and Sultan Qaboos University produced the 2018 book 'Barr Al Hikman: shorebird paradise in Oman'.
sites.sig: It is the single most important stop on the West Asian–East African flyway for Arctic-breeding shorebirds.
sites.ex: Environment Authority (Nature Reserves Section); Wetlands International, Radboud University, University of Groningen, NIOZ, Sultan Qaboos University
refs: Ramsar Convention (2023). Information Sheet on Ramsar Wetlands: Wetlands Reserve in Al Wusta Governorate (Barr Al Hikman), site 2529.
de Fouw, J., Bom, R., Thorpe, A., Klaassen, R. & Hagemeijer, W. (2018). Barr Al Hikman: shorebird paradise in Oman. Wetlands International.

sites.s: Grey-mangrove reserve inside Muscat · Ramsar site 2144
sites.p: Avicennia marina mangrove and tidal creek
sites.se: About 172 ha of grey mangrove in the heart of Muscat, protected since 1975, with 194 bird, 40 fish, 27 crustacean and 48 mollusc species
sites.sa: نحو 172 هكتاراً من أشجار القرم الرمادي في قلب مسقط، محمية منذ 1975، تضم 194 نوعاً من الطيور و40 من الأسماك و27 من القشريات و48 من الرخويات
sites.desc: Qurm Nature Reserve lies within the urban area of Qurm in Bawshar, Muscat, on the Sea of Oman, and takes its name from the grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) that dominates it. It was established in 1975 by decree of Sultan Qaboos, recognised as an Important Bird Area in 1994, and its lower 106.8 ha were designated Ramsar site 2144 on 19 April 2013; the whole reserve covers about 172 ha. The Ramsar record lists 194 bird species, more than 40 fish species including commercial ones, 27 crustaceans and 48 molluscs, and calls it one of the largest mangrove areas on the east coast of the Arabian Peninsula. It is being developed as a conservation and education site with a visitor centre.
sites.sig: It is the largest natural mangrove stand on Oman's northern coast and a nursery for the capital's fisheries.
sites.ex: Environment Authority of Oman; vegetation studied by H. Kürschner (1986)
disc: 106.8 ha Ramsar site inside the city
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Qurm Nature Reserve, site 2144 (2013).
Kürschner, H. (1986). A Study of the Vegetation of the Qurm Nature Reserve. Arab Gulf Journal of Scientific Research.
Wikipedia contributors (2026). Qurm Nature Reserve, citing RSIS and BirdLife International.

sites.s: Arabian tahr stronghold in the Eastern Hajar · UNESCO biosphere reserve 2025
sites.te: The shy goat of the cliffs
sites.se: A 1,039 km² mountain reserve 45 km south-west of Muscat set up in 1975 for the Arabian tahr, with 400 plant species, ten of them endemic
sites.sa: محمية جبلية بمساحة 1,039 كم² على بعد 45 كم جنوب غرب مسقط أُنشئت عام 1975 للطهر العربي، فيها 400 نوع نباتي عشرة منها متوطنة
sites.desc: Al Sireen Nature Reserve was set up in 1975 in the Eastern Hajar about 45 km south-west of Muscat, bordering the wilayats of Al Amerat, Qurayat and Dima wa Tayeen, with entry points at Jabal Aswad and Jabal Abyad. It covers 103,888 ha and is an IUCN Category II protected area. Its flagship species is the Arabian tahr, the smallest of the ibex-like goats, which hides among large rocks, can go two or three days without drinking and is threatened by poaching and urban expansion; Arabian gazelle, Arabian wolf, red fox, Egyptian vulture and the Oman saw-scaled viper also live there, with about 400 plant species including ten endemic and four endangered. In September 2025 UNESCO's MAB council added it, with Al Jabal al Akhdar, to the World Network of Biosphere Reserves, Oman's first; about 2,533 people live in its buffer zone.
sites.sig: It is the main protected refuge of the endangered Arabian tahr, found only in the Hajar mountains.
sites.ex: Environment Authority of Oman (Office for the Conservation of the Environment); UNESCO MAB
refs: Oman Observer (2024). Want to see a rare and shy animal? Come to Al Sireen Reserve.
Oman Observer (2025). Two Omani reserves listed on UNESCO's biosphere programme.

sites.s: Nine coastal lagoons protected since 1997 · Dhofar
sites.p: Brackish coastal lagoons with reed and mangrove
sites.se: A chain of nine brackish lagoons along the Dhofar coast, from Mughsayl to Khawr Rori, where migrants from Africa, Europe and India rest among reeds and mangroves
sites.sa: سلسلة من تسعة أخوار قليلة الملوحة على ساحل ظفار من المغسيل إلى خور روري، تستريح فيها الطيور المهاجرة من أفريقيا وأوروبا والهند بين القصب وأشجار القرم
sites.desc: The Dhofar government's protected region covers nine wetlands: Khawr Mughsayl, Khawr Dahareez, Khawr Baleed, Khawr Awqad, Khawr Sawli, Khawr Taqah, Khawr Rawri, Khawr Qurm al Sagheer and Khawr Qurm al Kabeer, declared protected in June 1997. They range from a few hectares to more than a hundred: Khawr Mughsayl is about 3 km long and 150 m wide, Khawr Awqad about 16 ha and Khawr Taqah about 2 km². More than 160 bird species have been recorded, the lagoons being important stopovers for migrants, with milkfish and mullet that tolerate changing salinity, reed-mace (Typha) and mangroves, which are being planted to give cover for birds. The management plan allows controlled fodder cutting and limited visitor facilities and protects the archaeological sites beside them.
sites.sig: Together the khawrs are the main freshwater-influenced bird habitat on Oman's monsoon coast.

sites.n: Hallaniyat Bay and the Arabian Sea humpback whale
sites.na: خليج الحلانيات والحوت الأحدب في بحر العرب
sites.s: Only non-migrating humpback population, fewer than 100 whales · Dhofar
sites.se: A tiny, isolated humpback population off Dhofar and the Gulf of Masirah that breeds and feeds in the same waters year-round and is now proposed as a fourth subspecies
sites.sa: مجموعة صغيرة معزولة من الحيتان الحدباء قبالة ظفار وخليج مصيرة تتكاثر وتتغذى في المياه نفسها طوال العام، ويُقترح الآن اعتبارها نويعاً رابعاً
sites.desc: The Oman Arabian Sea Important Marine Mammal Area covers 96,146 km² and holds the Arabian Sea humpback whale, estimated by mark-recapture at 82 individuals (95% CI 60–111) from 2000–2004 photo-identification, the basis of its IUCN Endangered listing. Satellite tags on 14 whales in 2014–2015 showed strong fidelity to two hotspots, Dhofar (Hallaniyat Bay), linked to reproduction, and the Gulf of Masirah, linked to feeding; at least 20 cetacean species use the area, including blue, Bryde's and sperm whales. Unlike other humpbacks they do not migrate. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Marine Science led by the Wildlife Conservation Society and the Environment Society of Oman, analysing mitochondrial DNA from 2,285 whales, found the population diverged 43,000–113,000 years ago, has the lowest genetic diversity of any humpback region and merits recognition as a fourth subspecies; threats include fishing-gear entanglement, vessel strikes and noise.
sites.sig: It is the world's only resident, non-migratory humpback whale population, and one of its smallest.
sites.ex: Environment Society of Oman; Wildlife Conservation Society; IUCN Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force
disc: About 82 whales, isolated for up to 113,000 years

sites.s: Acacia woodland and Arabian gazelle herds · Al Kamil wal Wafi
sites.p: Samr (Acacia tortilis) savanna on gravel plain
sites.se: A 220 km² acacia plain in Sharqiyah, protected in 1997, where Arabian gazelle herds have recovered from over-hunting among 57 bird and 166 insect species
sites.sa: سهل من السمر بمساحة 220 كم² في الشرقية حُمي عام 1997، تعافت فيه قطعان الغزال العربي من الصيد الجائر وسط 57 نوعاً من الطيور و166 من الحشرات
sites.desc: Al Saleel Natural Park lies at Al Kamil wal Wafi in Ash Sharqiyah, bounded by a mountain range to the north, a plain reaching the Gehwan reserve to the east and Wadi Al Bathaa and the Sharqiya Sands to the south. Set up in 1997, it covers 220 km² predominantly forested with samr (umbrella thorn acacia) and salam (Acacia ehrenbergiana) among more than 100 plant species. Its Arabian gazelle, once sharply reduced by over-hunting, are now seen in large herds thanks to local cooperation against poaching; the reserve also records about 57 bird species including steppe eagle, Arabian ibex, red fox, Cape hare, eight reptiles and 166 insect species, and the Omani wild cat is listed among its rare species. Visitors need a permit from the Environment Authority.
sites.sig: It protects the largest acacia woodland of eastern Oman and one of the country's main gazelle populations.
disc: Gazelle herds recovered after poaching controls

sites.n: Al Jabal Al Akhdar and the Saiq Plateau
sites.s: Terraced rose gardens at 2,000 m · UNESCO biosphere reserve 2025
sites.se: A high limestone plateau where falaj-fed terraces grow roses for rosewater, pomegranates and walnuts, home to wild olive, Arabian ibex and 71 bird species
sites.sa: هضبة جيرية عالية تروي أفلاجها مدرّجات الورد لصناعة ماء الورد والرمان والجوز، وتعيش فيها الزيتون البري والوعل العربي و71 نوعاً من الطيور
sites.desc: Al Jabal Al Akhdar in Ad Dakhiliyah is a mostly limestone massif about 150 km from Muscat whose Saiq plateau lies at about 2,000 m. Its mild, Mediterranean-type climate and mountain springs feed falaj channels and a centuries-old terrace system that grows roses for traditional rosewater, pomegranates, walnuts, apricots, grapes and peaches, and it is a major area for honey-bee breeding; rock-art figures about 6,000 years old have been studied on the mountain. In August 2011 a decree created the Jebel Akhdar Sanctuary for Natural Sceneries, and in September 2025 UNESCO's MAB council listed the Al Jabal al Akhdar Landscape, about 4,500 ha, as a biosphere reserve for its rare wild olive trees, threatened Arabian ibex and Arabian wolf and more than 71 bird species including Egyptian vulture and golden eagle.
sites.sig: It is Oman's highland agricultural heartland and, with Al Sireen, its first UNESCO biosphere reserve.
